FrMS88-de4350-d1e111.summary: Poses the eleventh question: whether the notion of being is the notion of a genus. Argument for: according to the Doctor two categories remain in God, substance and relation; similarly being could be a genus, and since it is predicated as ad se, its predication would be that of substance.
claims: Objection: if substance and relation remain in God, being could be a genus.

FrMS88-de4350-d1e124.summary: Contrary: Augustine says God is not in a genus. Meyronnes declares two truths, the first that being is not a genus. He rejects reasons from unlimitedness (animal would remain a genus even with infinite species), from quidditative predication of differences (shown false earlier), and from division by intrinsic modes (which do not impede quidditative predication). The whole reason is that being is not predicated in quid as an essential part, which is what the notion of genus first requires. Second truth: God is not in a genus; rejects the reasons from infinity (which would not exclude paternity, not formally infinite), from pure act (repugnance to a genus is prior to being act), and from composition (a thing in a genus need only have several formal notions, not compose them).
claims: Being is not a genus because it is not predicated in quid as an essential part.
Infinity, pure actuality, and composition are not the decisive reasons why God is not in a genus.
To be in a genus requires several formal notions, not composition.

FrMS88-de4350-d1e185.summary: Gives his own reason: whatever is in a genus includes the genus as an essential part, but it is repugnant to God to include anything superior as an essential part, since he is simply simple and irresolvable. Then raises four difficulties, the first: as being is predicated as a superior, does it have more the property of a genus or of a species?
claims: God is not in a genus because he is simply simple and irresolvable.

FrMS88-de4350-d1e201.summary: Answers that being is more like a species: a genus is predicated in quid of what adds to it a difference forming one formal notion, but an individual adds to its species only an individual property; likewise being is properly predicated in quid only of 'this being', which adds no formal notion to being.
claims: Being is predicated in quid properly only of 'this being', which adds only an individual property.
Being resembles a species more than a genus.

FrMS88-de4350-d1e224.summary: Second difficulty: whether being has its own individual in each thing.

FrMS88-de4350-d1e229.summary: Answers yes, and not only being but all transcendentals (one, true, good): things with distinct formal notions of themselves are distinguished in the same way wherever found, including in inferiors; so the transcendentals, distinguished in the abstract, are distinguished in each individual.
claims: Being and all transcendentals have their own individuals.
Formal notions distinct in superiors remain distinct in inferiors.

FrMS88-de4350-d1e249.summary: Third difficulty: whether being is said immediately of its inferiors. Answers yes, because an inferior adds to being only an intrinsic mode, and a formal notion is compared to its intrinsic mode prior to any other formal notion; haecceity seems to be nothing but the intrinsic mode of that whose haecceity it is.
claims: Being is said immediately of its inferiors, which add only an intrinsic mode.
Haecceity is an intrinsic mode.

FrMS88-de4350-d1e267.summary: Fourth difficulty: whether such an individual of being is in any category. Answers no: whatever is in a genus has the genus said of it in the first mode; since being and this being share a formal notion, whatever is said per se in the first mode of one is said of the other, so the genus would be said in quid of being itself, which is false.
claims: An individual of being is in no category.
concepts: first mode of per se predication

FrMS88-de4350-d1e289.summary: Raises the doubt whether everything in the categorial line also has its own individuals, and answers yes, by the same reasoning about distinct formal notions.
claims: Everything in the categorial line has its own individuals.

FrMS88-de4350-d1e298.summary: Draws from this a logicians' dictum: anything predicated of its own individual has more the character of a species than of a genus.
claims: A predicate said of its own individual has more the character of species than genus.

FrMS88-de4350-d1e306.summary: Reply to the opening argument: the Doctor never said there are two genera or categories in God, only two modes of predication.
claims: In God there are two modes of predication, not two categories.

FrMS88-de4350.summary: The eleventh question of the prologue asks whether the notion of being is the notion of a genus. Meyronnes declares two truths. First, being is not a genus: he rejects the usual reasons (unlimitedness, quidditative predication of differences, division by intrinsic modes) as inconclusive and gives the whole reason as this — being is not predicated in quid as an essential part, which is what the notion of a genus primarily requires. Second, God is not in a genus: rejecting arguments from infinity (which would not exclude paternity), pure act, and composition (a thing in a genus need only have several formal notions, not parts), he argues that whatever is in a genus includes it as an essential part, which is repugnant to the simply simple and irresolvable God. He then resolves four difficulties: being, as predicated of inferiors, is more like a species than a genus, since what it is said of in quid adds only an individual property; being and all transcendentals (one, true, good) have their own individuals, since distinctions among formal notions recur in their inferiors; being is said immediately of its inferiors, which add only an intrinsic mode (even haecceity being an intrinsic mode); and an individual of being is not in any category, since being would then be said of it in the first mode. Everything in the categorial line also has its own individuals, confirming the logicians' dictum that a predicate taken of its individual has more the character of species than genus. The opening appeal to the Doctor is answered: he spoke of two modes of predication in God, not two categories.
claims: Being is not a genus because it is not predicated in quid as an essential part.
God is not in a genus because he is simply simple and includes nothing superior as an essential part.
A thing in a genus need not be composite; it suffices that it have several formal notions.
Being, as predicated of its individuals, resembles a species more than a genus.
Being and the other transcendentals have their own individuals.
Being is said immediately of its inferiors, which add only intrinsic modes; haecceity is an intrinsic mode.
An individual of being is in no category.
